video.title: Coiling | Spinal Motion | Eye Dominance | Arm Slot - 15 Serves Explained

classification.reason: The coach provides actionable cues such as throwing the chest to the sky and technical adjustments like the pure-dextral pinpoint footwork for right-eye dominant servers.

problem.title_as_question: How should players adapt their serve mechanics and coiling to their ocular dominance and spinal mobility?
problem.definition: Players often copy aesthetic pro motions like Roger Federer's without realizing that ocular dominance and individual spinal mobility dictate how they must coil, track the court, and align their arm slot.
problem.target_player: Players struggling with serve accuracy, power, or awkward alignment, especially right-eye dominant players

quotes.text: So, we're going to start with Ben Shelton serve because I believe he has the best mechanics on the ATB Tour right now.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The first is coiling. And when we say coiling, what we mean is stretching the off shoulder against the hitting side hip.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: and then having that unwind through contact, you get more upward acceleration. And then the other thing I want you to notice is this thoracic extension we get here.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The thing that I want to mention though is that arm slot, absolute arm slot with respect to the ground is not as important as keeping your arm in the same plane of rotation as your shoulders.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: In general, if you keep your arm in line with your shoulders, everything is going to work a lot more effortlessly.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now, a lot of people overrate the role of forearm rotation, pronation and supernation, specifically pronation on the surf. It is not that important.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Shoulder rotation is what drives serve velocity. Now, he pronates a little, but that that's not that important.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And you should only be using federers if your body, your mobility, and one other thing we're about to talk about are the same as federers.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Roger Federer's dominant eye is his left eye. That is the eye that is towards the court. When you are serving, you must be able to see the service box and your opponent in your peripheral vision.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And players who are right eye dominant copy federous serve. They're using this eye. They have no peripheral awareness of what's going on here at all and they can't aim and the serve will forever feel awkward.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: It is an objective disadvantage to be purextral on serve. Being cross-dextral on serve is objectively better.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And so the only way to to meet both of those criteria is to allow yourself to fall off to the left and rotate.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: and if you've never felt this, if you're a right eye dominant player and you've never felt this, you've got to try serving more forward. All of a sudden, your accuracy is going to go way up.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: which is what I call the purodextral pinpoint. And I want you to look at the way he does this pinpoint. So, watch the back foot. He steps onto the right, the hitting side of his off foot.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If you're already serving pinpoint and you're right eye dominant, try this pinpoint because you're going to be able to coil your shoulder against your hip a lot more without having to turn so far away from the court.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: These have to be in the same plane of rotation to make the serve maximally comfortable, maximally efficient.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Yes, the legs add 10, 20%. And if your upper body mechanics are already perfect, then the legs are where you go. But most of the people watching this, your upper body mechanics are far from perfect.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: I want to work on one of the cues that I find helps people really get there and it's to throw your chest to the sky.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: A lot of people when they throw, they just don't really really have an internalization of getting that throwing motion to be an upward throwing motion. Lots of throws are forward throwing motions.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So take your chest, throw it to the sky. When you rotate, you're not twisting forward. You're twisting diagonally up and forward.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Just take your arm, put it back in the 9090 position. Very simple, just place it there. You don't need to momentum your way.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: but at some point you need to connect the serve to the act of receiving the first ball. And this where you finish, you land, you get wide, you split, and then you react and you track and receive
quotes.speaker: coach

symptoms.description: Right-eye dominant servers lack peripheral awareness of the service box and opponent during trophy phase and feel awkward aiming.
Server visibly falls off to the left on the landing after contact instead of jumping straight forward into court.
Serve lacks explosive pace despite aggressive forearm pronation effort.

causes.statement: The hitting arm swings out of the rotational plane of the shoulders, sacrificing rotational velocity and mechanical efficiency.
Right-eye dominant players turn their chest away from the court during coiling, cutting off peripheral vision of the service box and opponent.
Players attempt to generate power through forearm pronation rather than spring-loading the trunk and rotator cuff stretch-shortening cycle.
Players execute a forward horizontal throwing twist rather than extending the spine diagonally upward into the ball.

angles.summary: Serve velocity is primarily driven by spring-loaded trunk and shoulder stretch-shortening cycles rather than forearm pronation or leg drive.
High contact points require shoulder-over-shoulder cartwheeling so that the arm stays in the same rotational plane as the shoulders.
Copying Roger Federer's deep coiling turn is counterproductive for right-eye dominant servers because it blinds their peripheral vision.
Jakub Mensik and دیگر pure-dextral servers step the back foot to the hitting side to coil the trunk while keeping head and chest forward.
Throwing the chest to the sky directs the swing diagonally upward instead of twisting forward like a baseball pitch.

solutions.summary: If right-eye dominant, keep your head and chest facing more forward during windup to preserve peripheral court sightline.
Adopt the pure-dextral pinpoint stance by bringing the back foot onto the hitting side to stretch the shoulder against the hip without turning away.
solutions.external_goal: Step back foot onto the hitting side of the front foot

solutions.summary: Cue yourself to 'throw your chest to the sky' during upward drive to spring-load thoracic extension rather than rotating horizontally.
Simplify early preparation by manually placing the arm into a 90-90 trophy position if continuous momentum into external rotation disrupts timing.
